However, the model-specific characteristics of the underlying LLMs should also be considered when interpreting these findings. Although multiple LLMs were employed to mitigate the influence of model-specific characteristics, differences across models in instruction-following capability, response consistency, and the tendency to generate semantic variation may have affected the extent to which the assigned personality and belief conditions were reflected in actual agent responses. Differences in reasoning capability and response stability may also have influenced the processes of idea exploration and consensus formation. Therefore, the observed performance differences should be interpreted with consideration of the possibility that both agent diversity and the characteristics of the underlying models contributed to the results. Nevertheless, the systematic performance differences observed across diversity conditions under the same experimental structure suggest that, in addition to the choice of the underlying model, the composition of the agent group is an important design factor affecting collective decision-making performance in multi-agent systems.

sec.title: 6.2. Theoretical Contributions
sec.p: The theoretical contributions of this study are as follows. First, this study applied organizational diversity theory to research on LLM-based multi-agent systems, showing that the three dimensions of diversity discussed in human organization studies—variety, separation, and disparity—can be extended as design variables for artificial agent groups. Existing studies on multi-agent LLM systems have primarily focused on role allocation, discussion structures, prompt design, and self-review mechanisms. In contrast, this study is distinctive in that it systematically analyzed how the compositional diversity of agent groups themselves affects decision-making performance.

Second, this study extended the evaluation of multi-agent decision-making performance beyond single measures such as accuracy or final consensus achievement, proposing a multidimensional performance framework consisting of Idea Exploration Extent, Consensus Quality, and Consensus Efficiency. This reflects the idea that what matters in multi-agent decision-making is not merely reaching consensus quickly, but converging toward stable and efficient judgment while exploring diverse possibilities. Accordingly, this study contributes to LLM-based collective decision-making research by expanding performance evaluation from outcome-centered assessment to process- and balance-oriented assessment.

Third, this study empirically demonstrated that the relationship between diversity and decision-making performance is not linear. The maximum diversity group D maximized Idea Exploration Extent but showed substantially lower Consensus Quality and Consensus Efficiency. By contrast, the homogeneous group H showed strong Consensus Quality and Consensus Efficiency but limited exploration. These results show that the effect of diversity in multi-agent LLM systems cannot be interpreted simply as “more diversity is better.” In particular, the Pareto frontier analysis revealed that different diversity conditions produce different performance balance points, suggesting that the optimal level of diversity in multi-agent system design may vary depending on the purpose of the task.

sec.title: 6.3. Practical Contributions
sec.p: This study provides the following practical implications for designing LLM-based multi-agent systems. First, simply assigning diverse personality personas to agents may not be sufficient to improve decision-making performance. In this study, the personality-based variety diversity conditions were not included in the Pareto frontier. This suggests that diversity in expression style or communication style alone may not be sufficient to secure substantive diversity in decision-making perspectives.

Second, diversity in beliefs and value orientations should be considered a key design variable in multi-agent systems. The finding that all B-series groups were included in the Pareto frontier indicates that assigning agents different judgment criteria and value frames can be effective in expanding idea exploration while maintaining a certain level of Consensus Quality. Therefore, in practical decision-support systems, it may be useful to combine agents that represent different value criteria, such as market orientation, stability, ethics, and innovation.

Third, the level of diversity in agent groups should be designed differently depending on the purpose of the task. For tasks where the discovery of new opportunities or strategic exploration is important, configurations with high exploration performance, such as D, B-2, or B-3, may be appropriate. By contrast, for tasks where fast and stable consensus is important, highly homogeneous configurations such as H may be more suitable. For tasks that require a balance between exploration and consensus, a low level of belief diversity, such as B-1, may be an effective alternative.

Fourth, influence asymmetry should be designed with caution. In recent LLM-based multi-agent systems, agent orchestration structures have been discussed as an important design approach, in which an orchestrator agent assigns roles to multiple sub-agents, integrates their responses, and coordinates the overall decision-making process. However, for such structures to function effectively, a balance is needed between the authority of the central coordinator and the independent judgment of individual agents. In this study, all C-series groups were classified as dominated groups, indicating that assigning high influence to a particular agent does not always lead to efficient decision-making. This means that in LLM-based multi-agent systems, when the judgment of a specific agent is excessively reflected, the advantages of collective intelligence—namely the independent presentation of diverse perspectives and mutual verification—may be weakened. Therefore, rather than allowing a single highly influential agent to strongly control the judgments of sub-agents, multi-agent systems should be designed so that the orchestrator performs procedural coordination while sufficiently incorporating dissenting opinions and alternative perspectives from individual agents.

sec.title: 6.4. Limitations and Future Research
sec.p: This study has the following limitations. First, the experiment was conducted using a specific decision-making task within a single task domain and was evaluated based on a specific Delphi benchmark. Therefore, the observed effects of agent diversity may partly depend on the structure and characteristics of the selected task and benchmark. This limits the external validity of the findings, and the results should not be directly generalized to all types of Delphi tasks or decision-making situations. Future research should extend the experiment to diverse task domains, such as technology forecasting, policy decision-making, product planning, and risk assessment, and employ alternative benchmark tasks with different structures and levels of complexity to examine the robustness and generalizability of the observed diversity effects.

Second, this study manipulated agent diversity through prompts. Although personality, belief, and influence conditions were implemented through system prompts and response aggregation structures, it cannot be guaranteed that LLMs always internalize these instructions consistently. Future research should further examine the linguistic and behavioral characteristics of agent responses to verify the extent to which prompt-induced diversity is actually reflected in response patterns.

Third, this study used the level of alignment with a human expert benchmark as part of external consensus quality. However, given the nature of Delphi research, the consensus results of human experts should also be understood not as an absolute ground truth, but as a consensus-based criterion derived from the judgments of a specific expert group. Therefore, future research should extend the evaluation of external validity by using multiple human expert groups, independent evaluators, or actual ex post performance data.

Fourth, the Pareto frontier analysis in this study was conducted as a post-hoc analysis based on the observed results of predefined experimental groups. Therefore, this study did not automatically search for the optimal agent configuration, but rather analyzed the relative balance structures among the given diversity conditions. Future research should build on the findings of this study by treating the level of belief diversity, the number of agents, and the method of influence allocation as continuous design variables, and by using multi-objective optimization methods to explore optimal agent configurations according to task objectives.

Fifth, all experimental groups in this study were fixed at eight agents to maintain consistency in the evaluation conditions with the human expert benchmark study. Accordingly, this study did not examine the effect of group size itself on idea exploration, consensus quality, or consensus efficiency. Because increasing or decreasing the number of agents may alter the distribution of perspectives, response dispersion, and the consensus formation process within a group, future research should treat the number of agents as an independent experimental variable. Further investigation of the interaction between group size and diversity structure is also needed to identify agent-group configurations appropriate for different task objectives.
